title: Job queues
description: Job queues decouple 'request the work' from 'do the work': producers enqueue jobs, workers consume them, and the queue persists in between. The queue is durable (survives restarts), ordered (FIFO or priority), and observable (depth, age). Everything slow — exports, emails, renders — goes through the queue, never the request thread.
mechanism: Enqueue {type, payload, options} -> durable store -> workers poll/consume -> ack on done. Depth/age metrics. Dead-letter on repeated failure.
demo:
from collections import deque
import json

queue = deque()  # durable in production (Redis/DB)
dlq = []

def enqueue(job_type, payload):
    queue.append({'type': job_type, 'payload': payload, 'tries': 0})
    return 'enqueued (depth=%d)' % len(queue)

def worker():
    job = queue.popleft()
    print('worker: %s %s' % (job['type'], job['payload']))
    return 'acked'

print(enqueue('export', {'format': 'csv'}))
print(enqueue('email', {'to': 'jo@example.com'}))
print(worker(), '| remaining:', len(queue))
print('slow work NEVER on the request thread')

title: Workers
description: Workers execute the jobs: processes or threads pulling from the queue, running the handler, and acking. The pool scales with depth (autoscale on queue age), handlers are idempotent (redelivery is normal), and crashes are contained (one bad job doesn't kill the pool). Concurrency per worker matches the work (I/O-bound: many; CPU-bound: cores).
mechanism: Pool of consumers; prefetch limits; idempotent handlers; per-job timeouts; autoscale on depth/age. Crash isolation per job.
demo:
import concurrent.futures, time

def handle(job):  # idempotent handler (redelivery-safe)
    time.sleep(0.05)
    return 'done:%s' % job

jobs = ['j1', 'j2', 'j3', 'j4']
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=2) as pool:
    for result in pool.map(handle, jobs):
        print(result)
print('pool sized to the work (I/O: many threads; CPU: ~cores)')
print('handlers IDEMPOTENT: redelivery is normal, not exceptional')

title: Scheduling
description: Scheduling runs jobs later: delay (in 5 minutes), cron (every Monday 9am), and recurring intervals. The scheduler is durable (survives restarts — schedules in the DB, not memory) and exactly-once-ish (idempotent jobs make duplicates harmless). Timezones are explicit; DST is handled by the library, not by hope.
mechanism: Schedule store (DB); due jobs enqueued by the scheduler tick; idempotent handlers absorb duplicates. Cron with explicit timezone.

title: Retries
description: Retries handle transient failure: exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s...), jitter (avoid thundering herds), max attempts, then the dead-letter queue. Only retryable errors retry (timeouts yes, bad input no). The retry policy is per job type — payments retry differently than thumbnails. Idempotency makes retries safe.
mechanism: Backoff with jitter; max attempts; DLQ after; retryable vs fatal classification per error. Alert on DLQ growth.

title: Progress UI
description: Progress UI shows background work honestly: determinate bars (parts done/total), stage labels ('rendering page 3/12'), ETA from measured rate, and completion states. mechanism: Jobs report progress (done/total + stage); UI polls or streams; task center aggregates. ETA from rate. Cancel/retry per job.
algo: O(jobs) list; progress O(1) per update.

title: Cancellation
description: Cancellation stops jobs cleanly: the cancel signal reaches the worker, the handler checkpoints and exits, partial outputs are cleaned up, and the job records 'cancelled' (not 'failed'). Cooperative cancellation (the handler checks periodically) beats killing — killed jobs leave messes. Cancel must work at every stage: queued (just dequeue), running (signal), finishing (let it land).
mechanism: Cancel flag per job; handlers check periodically; cleanup on cancel; status='cancelled'. Queued: dequeue. Running: cooperative signal.

title: Priorities
description: Priorities order the queue: user-facing jobs (exports the user waits for) before batch (nightly aggregates). The implementation is priority queues (or separate queues per priority with weighted workers). Starvation is the risk — low-priority jobs must still progress (weighted fair share, or aging). Priorities are few (3-4 levels); more is unmanageable.
mechanism: Priority field; weighted workers across queues; aging prevents starvation. 3-4 levels max. User-facing > interactive > batch.
algo: O(log n) priority dequeue; aging O(1).
demo:
import heapq

# (priority, age-seq, job): lower number = higher priority; aging prevents starvation
q = []
seq = [0]

def enqueue(job, prio):
    seq[0] += 1
    heapq.heappush(q, (prio, seq[0], job))

enqueue('nightly-agg', 3); enqueue('user-export', 1); enqueue('thumbnail', 2)
while q:
    prio, _, job = heapq.heappop(q)
    print('run %-12s (prio %d)' % (job, prio))
print('3-4 levels max; aging: old low-prio jobs rise (no starvation)')

title: Persistence of jobs
description: Jobs persist: the queue, the schedules, and the job records (status, progress, results) all survive restarts in durable storage. A crashed worker's jobs return to the queue (visibility timeout); a restarted scheduler resumes. The job record is the audit trail — who requested, what happened, how long. Durability is what makes 'background' trustworthy.
mechanism: Durable store (DB/Redis persist); visibility timeouts (unacked -> requeue); job records with full history. Restart = resume, not reset.
demo:
import json, time

# job record: durable, the audit trail
job = {'id': 'j1', 'type': 'export', 'status': 'running',
       'progress': (3, 12), 'history': [('queued', 0), ('started', 10)]}
store = {'jobs': {}}

def checkpoint(j):
    j['history'].append(('checkpoint', time.time()))
    store['jobs'][j['id']] = json.dumps(j)  # durable
    return 'persisted'

print(checkpoint(job))
print('crash: unacked jobs requeue (visibility timeout); restart resumes')
print('record = audit trail: who, what, how long')

title: Cron jobs
description: Cron jobs are recurring background work: the schedule (cron expression + timezone), the handler (idempotent), and the monitoring (did it run? did it succeed?). The failure modes are missed runs (scheduler down — needs its own monitoring) and overlapping runs (long job + short interval — use locking). Cron is simple; operating cron reliably is the work.
mechanism: Cron expression + tz; distributed lock per run (no overlaps); idempotent handlers; monitoring on (ran? succeeded? duration?). Alert on miss.
algo: O(1) per tick; locks prevent overlap.
demo:
# overlap protection: distributed lock per scheduled run
locks = {}

def cron_run(name):
    if locks.get(name):
        return 'SKIP: previous run still going (no overlap)'
    locks[name] = True
    try:
        return 'ran %s (idempotent handler)' % name
    finally:
        locks[name] = False

print(cron_run('nightly'))
locks['nightly'] = True
print(cron_run('nightly'))
print('monitor: did it run? succeed? how long? alert on MISS (scheduler down)')

title: Resource limits
description: Background jobs need resource limits: CPU/memory per job (a runaway export doesn't take the node), concurrency caps per type, and queue depth limits (reject with 429 when full, don't OOM). The limits are per job type — video renders get more than thumbnails. Exceeded limits fail the job cleanly with a clear message.
mechanism: Per-type CPU/mem caps; concurrency limits; queue depth -> 429 (backpressure to callers). Clear failure messages on limit hits.

title: Idempotency
description: Idempotent jobs produce the same result when run twice: the handler checks 'already done?' before doing, uses idempotency keys, and writes atomically. Redelivery, retries, and duplicate cron ticks all become harmless. Non-idempotent jobs (charge the card) need exactly-once machinery — far harder. Design for idempotency first; exactly-once only where money moves.
mechanism: Idempotency key per job; check-then-act; atomic writes. Exactly-once only for money (transactional outbox).
demo:
# idempotency key: run twice, effect once
store, done_keys = {}, set()

def handle(key, payload):
    if key in done_keys:
        return 'duplicate: already done (harmless)'
    store[payload['id']] = payload['value']  # atomic write
    done_keys.add(key)
    return 'done'

print(handle('k1', {'id': 'a', 'value': 1}))
print(handle('k1', {'id': 'a', 'value': 1}), '(redelivery)')
print('money moves -> exactly-once (outbox); everything else -> idempotent')

title: Scaling workers
description: Worker scaling matches capacity to queue depth: scale up when depth/age grows, down when idle. The metrics are queue age (latency signal) more than depth (a deep queue of tiny jobs is fine). Scale-to-zero for batch queues; minimum pools for latency-sensitive. Autoscaling is on age + throughput, with cooldowns to avoid flapping.
mechanism: Autoscale on queue age (primary) + depth; cooldowns; scale-to-zero for batch; min pool for interactive. Workers stateless (any worker, any job).
algo: O(1) scaling decisions; cooldowns prevent flap.

title: Testing background jobs
description: Background jobs are tested like the critical path they are: unit tests for handlers (idempotency: run twice, assert once), integration tests with a real queue (redelivery, ordering), failure injection (kill workers mid-job), and load tests (depth spikes). Time is faked (no real sleeps in tests). The retry/DLQ paths get tested — they're the paths that run in production incidents.
mechanism: Unit (handlers + idempotency) -> integration (real queue) -> chaos (kill workers) -> load (spikes). Fake time. Test the retry/DLQ paths.
